84facc5f36e5.title: Business Process candidate
84facc5f36e5.content: A set of activities and tasks performed in coordination to achieve a specified business objective, or to deliver value in a specific way to a health service user. In the context of digitizing care pathways, this could include “health service user registration” and “referrals”, for example (see section 3.3). Also called: business process . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8). Wording alternative in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A set of related activities or tasks performed together to achieve the objectives of the health programme area, such as registration, counselling and referrals (3)." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen.

b31803a49f16.content: Functional applications are application components that deliver a specific operational function within a defined domain. The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

909862e1416c.title: Digital Transformation candidate
909862e1416c.content: The process of digitally optimizing and driving systems-level changes by leveraging innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms to improve person-centred health systems. Digital technologies are used to fundamentally change and improve how health services are delivered and accessed across all health programme areas (12,14,15). Also called: digital transformation . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8); identical wording (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), which inverts the two sentences: "In the health context, using digital technologies to fundamentally change and improve how health services are delivered and accessed across all health programme areas (3, 4, 5). The process involves using innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms to achieve systems-level changes." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

9659bc7c8217.title: Client Registry (CR) candidate
9659bc7c8217.content: The Client Registry is the national authoritative source of health-specific person identity. It is the foundational health-sector component that maintains a unique, verifiable identity record for every person who accesses or is eligible to access health services within a jurisdiction. Also called: CR . Verbatim lead sentence from Appendix C (Client Registry, 1 What It Is). Also abbreviated CR in the OpenHIE requirement identifiers (CRF-*, CRWF-*) and downstream Digital Transformation Handbooks. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

38382b4fe54d.title: Enterprise Architecture (EA) candidate
38382b4fe54d.content: The organising logic for business processes and IT infrastructure reflecting the integration and standardisation requirements of the organisation's operating model. Also called: EA, enterprise architecture . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (11)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies that helps planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise such as a health system (1)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help implementers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (3)." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

d220abe42344.title: Registry candidate
d220abe42344.content: A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health products and/or the health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set. Also called: registry . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. 26a60b5dc045.title: Traceability candidate
26a60b5dc045.content: The ability to trace something. In some cases, it is interpreted as the ability to verify the history, location or application of an item by means of documented identification (14). Also called: traceability . SC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing the WHO policy paper on traceability of medical products, ref. 14). Internal/substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 4 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-054.md, p. 54, citing GS1): "Traceability is the ability to trace the history, application or location of an object. In a supply chain context, it is the ability to see the movement of health products across the supply chain." Shared across dth-sc, dth-pc, and dth-sfp; both definitions are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140).

000d4676d245.content: General attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. Examples of non-functional requirements include ability to work offline, multiple language settings, and password protection (see section 3.8). Also called: Non-functional requirements, nonfunctional requirements, NFR . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (without section cross-reference) in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary ('nonfunctional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of how the digital system needs to operate and perform in order to support the tasks that make up the business process." (2) PC handbook glossary ('Non-functional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of the attributes and constraints that the system must have to ensure its quality and performance. These requirements do not specify what the system should do, but rather how the system should perform its functions. (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to support offline mode when network connectivity is not available)" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

1e873a109f50.title: Governance candidate
1e873a109f50.content: Governance is the set of arrangements through which decision authority is distributed, exercised and accounted for across all those who depend upon, contribute to, or are served by the shared infrastructure. Also called: governance, governance (health supply chain) . RA §3.4.1 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-029-341-purpose-and-framing.md, p. 64–65). Substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 3 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-045.md, p. 45): "In the context of the health supply chain, governance is the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures and mechanisms to ensure that the supply chain processes and the systems to manage those processes are managed effectively, ethically and in alignment with established objectives and stakeholders’ interests." (RA defines governance as the distribution, exercise, and accountability of decision authority across shared infrastructure; SC defines it as the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures, and mechanisms for supply chain processes and systems.) Also related to `digital-health-governance` in Mehl et al. 2023 (glossary/full-stac.glossary.json, smart-ra#143 P8). Also framed in SFP handbook §2.3 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-015-23-establish-governance-and-leadership.md, page-028.md, p. 16) as a structure for coordinating multiple stakeholders, defining clear roles and responsibilities, enhancing transparency, and creating a stable platform for decision-making. Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140, dth-sfp#1 P2).

7bc4f11cbd80.title: Interoperability candidate
7bc4f11cbd80.content: Interoperability is the standards-based capability of heterogeneous information systems to communicate, exchange data, and use the exchanged information to execute functions effectively. Also called: interoperability . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and internal alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9), PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10): "Ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "The ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner, through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries. In the health context, this provides timely, safe and seamless portability of information to help ensure good health outcomes (1)." (3) PHC handbook §4.4 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, §4.4, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and standards, which should be defined by the EA and independent of a particular solution’s system architecture (22)." (4) PHC handbook §4.4.2 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and data representation standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

632ae99e7a0c.title: Evaluation candidate
632ae99e7a0c.content: The systematic and objective assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention with the aim of determining the fulfilment of objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability (8). Also called: evaluation . SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The systematic assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention to determine whether the intervention is fulfilling its objectives and to demonstrate an effect on health outcomes." Also contrasted with monitoring in SFP §6.1 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-029-61-develop-a-monitoring-and-evaluation-plan.md, page-051.md, p. 39, quoting Pritchett et al. 2013): "Evaluation asks whether the project is doing the right things, while monitoring asks whether the project is doing things right." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1).

34269fb28b67.title: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) candidate
34269fb28b67.content: A set of shared digital systems that should be secure and interoperable, and can be built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition, while respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms. (G20/UNDP) . Also called: DPI . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Wording alternative in RA §1.1.2 body (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-002-112-understanding-digital-public-infrastructure.md): "Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) refers to shared digital systems that are secure and interoperable, built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition and respect human rights and fundamental freedoms." (Glossary reads "interoperable, and can be built"; body reads "interoperable, built".) Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

25994fef837e.title: Trade Item candidate
25994fef837e.content: Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Also called: trade item, Trade item . Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition.

c7b506059805.title: SMART Guidelines (SMART) candidate
c7b506059805.content: Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital. Also called: SMART guidelines, SMART, Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11): "Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The WHO guidelines for developing Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable components for implementing digital health capabilities. The components include interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, and technical and operational specifications. The SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital (12, 13)." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "WHO standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based, and testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content. They represent a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.11, 12" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

a18f695b23eb.title: Actor (Conformance Model) candidate
a18f695b23eb.content: An Actor is an abstract, well-bounded role in the health information ecosystem that is defined entirely by the information-processing responsibilities it assumes and the interactions it participates in. An Actor is neither a software product nor an organisational unit. Also called: Actor, actor (conformance model) . Defined in RA §3.7.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-050-372-the-model.md, p. 111–116). Substantive distinction from the platform's `actor` concept in folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json ("A concrete participant, human, agentic or mechanical, that persists across every process and takes on roles"): the RA's conformance-model Actor is an abstract information-processing role realised by concrete systems, closer to IHE's Actor or the platform's Role (smart-ra#133 S1).

A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

79801f26e24c.title: Digital Health candidate
79801f26e24c.content: The systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science, and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce, and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness. Also called: digital health . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8, citing WHO Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020–2025): "Digital health is the systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science, and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce, and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness (11)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG and Global Strategy): "The systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness (1, 2)." (3) SC handbook Introduction (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-012.md, p. 12, quoting the WHO Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020–2025, same source cited by dth-hrh): "the field of knowledge and practice associated with the development and use of digital technologies to improve health". All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

d2a01a707e5e.title: Open Source candidate
d2a01a707e5e.content: Open-source software is software with source code that is published and made freely available to the public, enabling anyone to inspect, modify and enhance the code (18). While the source code is open to everyone, this does not mean that implementation of software is necessarily without costs. An open-source software must have a license approved by the Open Source Initiative (19). Also called: Open-source software, open-source software, open source . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary under 'open-source software' (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), which adds "within set guidelines": "Software with source code that is published and made freely available to the public so anyone can inspect, modify and enhance the code within set guidelines (8). While the source code is open to everyone, the implementation of the software is not necessarily without costs. Open-source software must have a license approved by the Open Source Initiative (9)." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Distinct from the RA's architectural `product` concept; both wordings are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142).

7a2bd106a42e.title: User Story (Requirements) candidate
7a2bd106a42e.content: Captures a long list of features from an end-user’s perspective. It describes who the end-user is, with their feature wants or needs, and the reason for that want or need (see section 3.2.3). Also called: User Story, user story . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11). Internal and platform alternatives (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) PHC handbook §3.2.3 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-013-32-get-to-know-the-users.md, pp. 33-35): "User stories are the start of generating a long list of requirements, in non-technical terms, that will help the technical team to determine the more specific functional requirements of the system." and the template "“As a… [user persona], I want to… [do what I want to be able to do differently using an electronic system], so that… [reason for wanting that functionality].”" (2) Platform glossary `user-story` (folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json), which binds the story to a Role rather than a user persona: "What a reader acting in a Role is trying to do, told as that role: as a <role>, I want <want>, so that <so that>." Also used as the functional requirements template ("As a … / I want … / So that ...") in SFP handbook §4.5 Table 12 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-026-45-gather-requirements.md, page-043.md, p. 31).

16e6ab0ce069.content: The Health Management Information System is a governed, shared application component responsible for the systematic collection, aggregation, analysis, and dissemination of population-level and facility-level health data to support health system planning, performance monitoring, resource allocation, and policy decision-making. Also called: HMIS . Lead sentence from Appendix C (Health Management Information System, 1 What It Is). Abbreviated HMIS throughout the RA draft and downstream Digital Transformation Handbooks. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

e0728db9cf40.title: Health Information System (HIS) candidate
e0728db9cf40.content: A system that integrates data collection, processing, reporting, and use of the information necessary for improving health service effectiveness and efficiency through better management at all levels of health services. Also called: HIS, health information system, Health Information System (HIS), Health Information Systems . DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO 2004 Developing health management information systems; also abbreviated in DIIG page-011.md and HRH handbook who-iris/library/9789240062627-eng/sections/page-006.md). The PHC handbook (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng) has no HIS abbreviation or definition; a wording earlier attributed to it here is not in its text and was removed (smart-ra#200). Referenced in SFP handbook glossary under SMART Guidelines (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) and Ch. 4 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-021-4-determine-the-requirements.md, page-035.md, p. 23). The definition is recorded as a candidate (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 P2).

069f9bafad03.title: Point-of-Service Applications (POS) candidate
069f9bafad03.content: Point-of-service applications are end-user application components (IT systems or software tools) used by individuals directly engaged in healthcare—such as clinicians, community health workers, and patients—that enable interaction with the broader healthcare ecosystem. Also called: POS, Point-of-service applications, Point of Service Application, PoS . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. The draft marks this entry [Under review]. Also categorized in SFP handbook §3.2 Fig. 3 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-020-32-link-to-the-enterprise-architecture.md, page-034.md, p. 22, citing DIIG) into reused POS applications and unique POS applications.

d9fe9e2de73c.title: Open Standards candidate
d9fe9e2de73c.content: Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20). Also called: open standards, Open standards . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10), and near-identical (two sentences) in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public. Open standards are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (10)." Substantive/complementary alternative in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, linked via exactMatch to glossary/full-stac.glossary.json): "Open standards are validated and vetted specifications, repeatedly reusableacross contexts, that address common requirements, processes, and interactions and enable fidelity metrics." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142 item 3, smart-ra#143).

5149dd17f621.content: Documentation, using open standards, of reusable enterprise architecture patterns for health systems, describing the diverse digital interconnections of systems and capabilities (including trust networks, services, registries, access controls). Open architectures are designed to be instantiable via open technologies; provide a core infrastructure that fosters an ecosystem of digital health tools; are developed and maintained through collaborative, consensus-driven processes; and are freely available for use and adaptation without license restrictions. a567cf654008.title: Full-STAC candidate
a567cf654008.content: Together, open Standards, open Technologies, open Architectures and open Content represent a next-generation ‘full-STAC’ remedy for digital health transformation. Also called: Full-STAC, full-STAC, full-STAC approach, full-STAC remedy . Quoted from the abstract. The paper calls it both an approach and a remedy, and names the four as 'four factors'. The DPI-H RA draft (sec-022, footnote 14) cites this paper and presents the four as 'the enabling conditions for REDDHI'.

9d0c75f0ec35.title: Open Content candidate
9d0c75f0ec35.content: Representations of public health, health system, or clinical knowledge, which are developed to meet the business needs described by an open architecture, and which describe, using open standards, assets such as minimum datasets, decision-support logic, care protocols, performance metrics, workflows, and reporting templates. Open content is developed, validated, and maintained through expert communities, and is freely available for use and adaptation without license restrictions. Transcribed from Figure 1 (p. 2). e2312e048353.content: Digital health governance defines who, what and how to govern to achieve health service impact. The paper cites Marcelo et al. 2018 (ADB) for this sentence, so the definition is that source's, as quoted here.

d7f084d5ee7d.title: Open Standards candidate
d7f084d5ee7d.content: Semantic and syntactic models for data representation, exchange, and processing that ensure the precise meaning of exchanged information is unambiguously interpretable by any other system, service, or user. Open standards are developed and maintained through collaborative, consensus-driven processes, and are freely available for use and adaptation without license restrictions. Transcribed from Figure 1 (p. 2). The figure's text is drawn as outlines, so the ingest could not extract it (vector-figures.json: vfig-p002 unrendered); the transcription was read off a 220 dpi render of the page on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. Example given in the figure: shared FHIR profiles with standard ontologies. The body text also says: 'OPEN STANDARDS refers to a common schema for health data, calculations and information exchange.' .

9c43fc1e29e4.title: A
9c43fc1e29e4.content: Access Point AP candidate A participating organisation's own connection point in a distributed model. Expanded and defined in the legend of Table 3.6 (Illustrative health information exchange mechanisms). A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/access-point · source folio/dpi-h-ra/ch3-the-reference-architecture-for-d/t-3-6.md . Actor (Conformance Model) candidate An Actor is an abstract, well-bounded role in the health information ecosystem that is defined entirely by the information-processing responsibilities it assumes and the interactions it participates in. An Actor is neither a software product nor an organisational unit. Defined in RA §3.7.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-050-372-the-model.md, p. 111–116). Substantive distinction from the platform's `actor` concept in folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json ("A concrete participant, human, agentic or mechanical, that persists across every process and takes on roles"): the RA's conformance-model Actor is an abstract information-processing role realised by concrete systems, closer to IHE's Actor or the platform's Role (smart-ra#133 S1). Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/actor-conformance-model · source library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-050-372-the-model.md . Adverse Events Following Immunization AEFI candidate Adverse effects following immunisation . Recorded per smart-ra#142 item 4: the PC handbook abbreviations list (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-006.md, p. 6) expands AEFI as "Adverse effects following immunisation", whereas standard WHO immunization terminology expands AEFI as "Adverse events following immunization" (an 'event' is any untoward medical occurrence following immunization and does not presuppose a causal 'effect'). Both expansions are recorded as candidates; neither is silently altered. b2930eac8ab2.content: Benefits Package Registry BPR candidate The Benefits Package Registry is the national authoritative record of all health benefit packages offered within a country's health financing ecosystem. It holds the definitive description of what each package covers, who is eligible in general terms, which scheme or schemes offer it, and under what rules and conditions benefits may be accessed. Verbatim lead sentences from Appendix C (Benefits Package Registry, 1 What It Is). Abbreviated BPR in the Appendix C comparison table. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Business Domain candidate A specific focus area or subsystem within a broader business system, characterized by its own essential attributes . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. The draft marks this entry [Under review]. Business Process candidate A set of activities and tasks performed in coordination to achieve a specified business objective, or to deliver value in a specific way to a health service user. In the context of digitizing care pathways, this could include “health service user registration” and “referrals”, for example (see section 3.3). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8). Wording alternative in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A set of related activities or tasks performed together to achieve the objectives of the health programme area, such as registration, counselling and referrals (3)." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen. Depicted in ArchiMate dpi-h-ra 0.3.0-draft.1: Business Process (BusinessProcess); views: Metamodel vs EIRA . Business Services Layer candidate A layer of the reference architecture grouping the health capabilities that national health systems strive to deliver across their principal domains — clinical care, public health, the health supply chain, and health financing — together with the shared components that enable them. 2be908c05bfe.content: Capability candidate A high-level ability the health system possesses or needs in order to achieve its goals. Enabling Environment candidate Attitudes, actions, policies and practices that stimulate and support effective and efficient functioning of organizations, individuals and programmes. The enabling environment includes legal, regulatory and policy frameworks and political, sociocultural, institutional and economic factors (3). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG), matching DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-139.md, p. 127). Shared DIIG Phase 1 concept across DTHs (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1); recorded as a candidate. Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/enabling-environment · source who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md . End-User candidate People who will be using the digital system(s). Identical wording in PHC handbook glossary ('End-user', who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8), PC handbook glossary ('End user', who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), and SFP handbook glossary ('End user', who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary ('end users', who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "People who will be using the digital systems." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1). Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/end-user · source who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md . Enterprise Architecture EA candidate The organising logic for business processes and IT infrastructure reflecting the integration and standardisation requirements of the organisation's operating model. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (11)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies that helps planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise such as a health system (1)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help implementers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (3)." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/enterprise-architecture · source folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md . Evaluation candidate The systematic and objective assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention with the aim of determining the fulfilment of objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability (8). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The systematic assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention to determine whether the intervention is fulfilling its objectives and to demonstrate an effect on health outcomes." Also contrasted with monitoring in SFP §6.1 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-029-61-develop-a-monitoring-and-evaluation-plan.md, page-051.md, p. 39, quoting Pritchett et al. 2013): "Evaluation asks whether the project is doing the right things, while monitoring asks whether the project is doing things right." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1). Candidate definitions (1) . | Monitoring (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)The continuous process of collecting and analysing data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results (8). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-141.md, p. 129, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The process of collecting and analysing routinely collected data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results and measure changes in performance over time." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1). | . a9f233952140.title: F
a9f233952140.content: Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources FHIR candidate FHIR is a standard for healthcare data exchange, published by HL7® . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/fast-healthcare-interoperability-resources · source folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md . Features candidate The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g. “reporting” can be a feature of a PCPOSS). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording alternatives across the DTH corpus, differing only in domain example and 'a system' vs 'your system' (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “order processing” can be a feature of an order management solution)." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The characteristics of your system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “approval workflow” can be a feature of a product master data management solution)." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Candidate definitions (2) . | Functions (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Functions in a system are how features are implemented (e.g. “calculating aggregate data” and “displaying feedback in the form of diagrams” are functions of the “reporting” feature of a PCPOSS). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Substantive alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Business processes within a system that help the system perform (e.g., “receiving inventory” and “picking inventory” are functions of the “warehousing” feature of a warehouse management system)." (PHC defines functions as "how features are implemented"; SC defines them as "Business processes within a system that help the system perform".) Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1). | Functional Requirements (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified health system challenges (e.g. a PCPOSS must be able to remind health workers which health service users to follow-up with). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording and substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the business process and address the identified challenges." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified challenges (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to define categories and attributes to organize product information)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Capabilities the system must have to meet the end users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. | . Foundational Digital Public Infrastructure DPI-F candidate Foundational Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-F) is the digital public infrastructure, such as identity, payments and data exchange, upon which the health sector can build. DPI-H is distinct from DPI-F and builds on it. Added to the RA glossary table in CS-001 (smart-ra#185, public comments No. 136 and No. 327), per committee feedback (CL). A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Named in the RA draft's Acronyms table, which gives the expansion used as prefLabel, and in Section 1.2.3 on cross-sectoral foundational DPI (digital identity, payments, data exchange). Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/foundational-digital-public-infrastructure · source folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md . Full-STAC candidate An ecosystem specifying open standards, open technologies, open architectures, and open content (full-STAC). Cites Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json) in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#143). Candidate definitions (4) . | Open Standards (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10), and near-identical (two sentences) in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public. Open standards are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (10)." Substantive/complementary alternative in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, linked via exactMatch to glossary/full-stac.glossary.json): "Open standards are validated and vetted specifications, repeatedly reusableacross contexts, that address common requirements, processes, and interactions and enable fidelity metrics." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142 item 3, smart-ra#143). | Open Technologies (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open technologies denote components of configurable and extensible source code — often curated as digital public goods — that perform distinct functions while adhering to open standards. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Components of configurable and extensible source code, often curated as 'global goods' or 'digital public goods', that perform a distinct function while adhering to open standards."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | Open Architectures (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open architectures refer to high-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "High-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components, such as within a health information exchange."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | Open Content (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open content refers to domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage, such as health guidelines, workflows, core data elements, terminology mappings, and test cases aligned to standards."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | . Full-STAC candidate Together, open Standards, open Technologies, open Architectures and open Content represent a next-generation ‘full-STAC’ remedy for digital health transformation. Quoted from the abstract. The paper calls it both an approach and a remedy, and names the four as 'four factors'. The DPI-H RA draft (sec-022, footnote 14) cites this paper and presents the four as 'the enabling conditions for REDDHI'. 854abfd7e39f.title: G
854abfd7e39f.content: Generic Product candidate In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Internal wording alternative in PC handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28): "Generic products can be described as generic items that conceal the brand or manufacturer information." Distinct from the RA's architectural `product` concept; both wordings are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142). Candidate definitions (2) . | Trade Item (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition. | Product Master Data (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Product master data consists of standardized information that accurately describes a health product’s characteristics. This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#141, smart-ra#142): one concept, with no homonym split needed against the RA's architectural `product` concept. | . Governance candidate Governance is the set of arrangements through which decision authority is distributed, exercised and accounted for across all those who depend upon, contribute to, or are served by the shared infrastructure. RA §3.4.1 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-029-341-purpose-and-framing.md, p. 64–65). Substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 3 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-045.md, p. 45): "In the context of the health supply chain, governance is the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures and mechanisms to ensure that the supply chain processes and the systems to manage those processes are managed effectively, ethically and in alignment with established objectives and stakeholders’ interests." (RA defines governance as the distribution, exercise, and accountability of decision authority across shared infrastructure; SC defines it as the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures, and mechanisms for supply chain processes and systems.) Also related to `digital-health-governance` in Mehl et al. 2023 (glossary/full-stac.glossary.json, smart-ra#143 P8). Also framed in SFP handbook §2.3 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-015-23-establish-governance-and-leadership.md, page-028.md, p. 16) as a structure for coordinating multiple stakeholders, defining clear roles and responsibilities, enhancing transparency, and creating a stable platform for decision-making. Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140, dth-sfp#1 P2). The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. | . 0990166274b6.content: Open Architectures candidate Open architectures refer to high-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "High-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components, such as within a health information exchange."). Candidate definitions (4) . | Full-STAC (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)An ecosystem specifying open standards, open technologies, open architectures, and open content (full-STAC). Cites Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json) in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#143). | Open Standards (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10), and near-identical (two sentences) in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public. Open standards are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (10)." Substantive/complementary alternative in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, linked via exactMatch to glossary/full-stac.glossary.json): "Open standards are validated and vetted specifications, repeatedly reusableacross contexts, that address common requirements, processes, and interactions and enable fidelity metrics." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142 item 3, smart-ra#143). | Open Technologies (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open technologies denote components of configurable and extensible source code — often curated as digital public goods — that perform distinct functions while adhering to open standards. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Components of configurable and extensible source code, often curated as 'global goods' or 'digital public goods', that perform a distinct function while adhering to open standards."). Candidate definitions (2) . | Generic Product (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Registry candidate A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health products and/or the health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set. (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health products and/or the health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores, and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, products and/or health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set." (4) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10, truncated in source PDF): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, products and/or health workforce using predefined canonical minimum data etc." All five are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. SMART Guidelines SMART candidate Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11): "Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The WHO guidelines for developing Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable components for implementing digital health capabilities. The components include interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, and technical and operational specifications. The SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital (12, 13)." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "WHO standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based, and testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content. They represent a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.11, 12" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Traceability candidate The ability to trace something. In some cases, it is interpreted as the ability to verify the history, location or application of an item by means of documented identification (14). SC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing the WHO policy paper on traceability of medical products, ref. 14). Internal/substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 4 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-054.md, p. 54, citing GS1): "Traceability is the ability to trace the history, application or location of an object. In a supply chain context, it is the ability to see the movement of health products across the supply chain." Shared across dth-sc, dth-pc, and dth-sfp; both definitions are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140). Trade Item candidate Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition. Candidate definitions (2) . | Generic Product (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Internal wording alternative in PC handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28): "Generic products can be described as generic items that conceal the brand or manufacturer information." Distinct from the RA's architectural `product` concept; both wordings are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142). | Product Master Data (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Product master data consists of standardized information that accurately describes a health product’s characteristics. This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#141, smart-ra#142): one concept, with no homonym split needed against the RA's architectural `product` concept. | . df257caa1c31.title: Already somebody else’s concept?
df257caa1c31.content: Extracted candidates are minted from this repository’s own assets and are not, by themselves, checked against any vocabulary. check:term-mapping asks whether each already exists as a concept somebody is authoritative for — SKOS for what a term MEANS, FHIR for a clinical code’s operational semantics — and the two are separate questions with separate answers. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 4 | 202 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 206 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin.
